caseno: Civil Petition for Leave to Appeal No. 27 of 2002
lawyer:
AKM Nazrul  Islam, Senior Advocate instructed by Sharif uddin Chaklader; Advocate-on-Record ----- For the Petitioners. 
KZ Alam, Senior Advocate, instructed by Md Aftab Hossain. Advocate-on-Record ----- For Respondent No. 1.
Not Represented ----- Respondent Nos. 2-9.
parties:
Shishir Kanti Pal and others  ----- Petitioners 
Vs.
Nur Muhammad and others  ----- Respondents
case_source: (From the Judgment and Order dated July 10, 2001 passed by the High Court Division in Civil Revision No. 110 of 1994).
full_judgment:
Md. Ruhul Amin J: This petition for leave to appeal is against the judgment and order of July 10, 2001 of a Single Bench of the High Court Division in Civil Revision No. 110 of 1994 discharging the Rule. The civil revision was filed against the judgment and decree of 31st October, 1993 of the Court of District Judge, Lakshmipur in Title Appeal No. 44 of 1999 allowing the appeal and consequent thereupon decreeing the suit upon reversing the judgment and decree dated April 30, 1981 of the Court of Subordinate Judge, Noakhali in Other Class Suit No. 85 of 1967 dismissing the same. The suit was filed seeking declaration that the property in suit described in the schedule 'A' to the plaint was not enemy property and that the notification dated July 31, 1965 published in the Dhaka Gazette dated November 4, 1965 notifying the property as evacuee/enemy property, illegal, without jurisdiction and not binding upon the plaintiffs.

2. The plaintiffs are claiming the property as described in schedule 'A' to the plaint on the basis of exchange with the property described in schedule 'B' to the plaint. Property described in schedule Ato the plaint belonged to erstwhile East Pakistanis ie defendant Nos. 5-12 and the property described in schedule 'B' belonged to the plaintiffs, the migrants from the Tripura State, India. Plaintiffs instituted. the suit stating, inter alia, that they were the inhabitants of Tripura State in India and they upon exchanging their property described in schedule 'B' in the Indian State of Tripura with property in erstwhile East Pakistan as described in schedule 'A' to the plaint migrated to erstwhile East Pakistan in the year 1963 and that got possession of the property as described in schedule 'A' to the plaint, that the property was exchanged by an irrevocable Power of Attorney which was registered on May 24, 1963 in the office of the Munsif-cum-Magistrate, 1st Class, Udaypur, Tripura, that on their corning over to then East Pakistan they submitted the said Irrevocable Power of Attorney in the form of exchange deed in the Office of the Deputy Commissioner, (Revenue) Comilla and the same was duly re-stamped by the Deputy Commissioner, Comilla. It is also the case of the plaintiffs that they migrated to then Pakistan in the month of August, 1963 and pursuant to the deed of exchange they got the possession of the exchanged properties described in the schedule 'A' to the plaint and that are in possession thereof. Further case of the plaintiffs is, that some greedy persons of the locality to grab the properties on denial of the right of the plaintiffs got the properties described in schedule 'A' declared as evacuee/enemy property by the notification dated July 31, 1965 published in the Gazette on November 4, 1965 and while the persons who got the property declared evacuee/enemy property tried to take lease of the property from the office of the Deputy Commissioner, Noakhali the plaintiffs were constrained to file the suit.

3. The suit was contested by the defendant No.1 Government of Bangladesh, Defendant No.5, Defendant No. 6 and Defendant Nos. 7-12.

4. The case of the defendant No. 5 was that his father Chandra Kumar Pal was .the owner of 11.77 acres of land of Khatian Nos. 30 and 32 (from amongst the property as described in schedule 'A') and that his father died leaving him and another as sons and his brother; sold his share in the aforementioned property to him and that he and his brother sold 1-26 acres of land to some others. It is also the case of the defendant that neither he nor his brother executed the deed. of exchange in the form of irrevocable power of attorney and that the alleged deed of exchange in the form of power of attorney is forged, fraudulent and fabricated and that the plaintiffs were never the owners and possessors of the property described in schedule 'B' and that he and others had never exchanged their properties as described in. schedule 'A' with the property described-in schedule 'B'. It was also contended that the plaintiffs were never the inhabitants of Tripura State and that they being the inhabitants of Noakhali used to go to Tripura State for seasonal employment in an agriculture firm. The further contention of the defendant No.5 is that the property of Khatian Nos. 30 and 32 cannot be treated as enemy property.

5. The case of the defendant No.6 was that his father Puma Chandra Pal was the owner of the land recorded in khatian Nos. 29, 94, 100 and 255 as mentioned in schedule 'A' and that his father died leaving 3 sons including him and that his 2 brothers upon transferring their shares to him left the then East Pakistan and living in West Bengal and that his brothers were never in the Tripura State and that he and his brothers had never executed the power of attorney for the purpose of exchanging schedule 'A' land for 'B' schedule land and that the power of attorney is forged, fabricated and fraudulent and thus his property cannot be treated as enemy property.

6. The case of the defendant Nos. 7-12 was that part of the land of Khatian Nos. 30, 50, 52, 53, 55,95 and 94 as mentioned in schedule 'A' belonged to Raj Kumar Pal, Rajani Kumar Pal, Chandra Kumar Pal and Ram Sundar (Kumar) Pal, that Raj Kumar Pal died leaving 3 sons-defendant No.9, defendant No. 10 and another by name Anukul Chandra Pal who transferred his share to the defendant Nos. 9 and 10 and left for India, Rajani Kumar died leaving 2 sons-defendant No.7 and another by name Gopal Pal who transferred his share to the defendant No.7. Chandra Kumar died leaving 3 sons defendant No. 8 and two others by name, Chitta Ranjan Pal and SushiI Pal and the said two brothers ie Chitta Ranjan Pal and Sushil Pal, transferred their shares to defendant No.8 and left the then East Pakistan for India, Ram Kumar Pal died leaving 4 sons-defendant Nos. 11, 12 and two others by name Harihar and Fani Bhusan Pal and that Harihar and Fani Bhusan transferred their share to the defendant Nos. 11 and 12 and left the then East Pakistan for India. It is the case by this set of defendants that they are in possession of their land acquired by inheritance and purchase and that their property as described in schedule 'A' to the plaint cannot be treated as evacuee or enemy property and that they had never executed the power of attorney in the form of deed of exchange in respect of schedule 'A' property for the property described in schedule ‘B’.

7. The case of the defendant No.1 is that the property described in schedule 'A' belonged to the recorded Hindu owners and they being absent from the then East Pakistan and that as they were staying in India at the relevant time as well as at the time of Promulgation of Defence of Pakistan Ordinance, 1965 and the Rules framed thereunder the property of the said recorded tenants assumed the character of evacuee/enemy property and thereupon the properties of the recorded tenants were declared evacuee/enemy property through the notification dated 31-7-1965 and publication thereof in Hie Gazette of dated 4th November, 1965. This defendant has denied the case of the plaintiffs ie exchange of their properties in India as described in schedule 'B' with properties as described in schedule 'A' to the plaint. It was further contended by the defendant that the deed of exchange in the form of irrevocable power of attorney was forged and fabricated and that the plaintiffs were never the inhabitants of Tripura State, India and that taking advantage of the absence of the recorded owners of the property described in schedule 'A' the plaintiffs brought into existence forged and fabricated exchange deed to grab the property described in schedule A and that by the Exhibit 1-irrevocable, power. of attorney plaintiffs have not acquired any interest in the properties described in schedule A and that they are not in possession of the properties of schedule 'A'.

8. It may be mentioned the suit was finally contested by the defendant No.1 Government of Bangladesh and defendant No.5 Rashamoy Pal who figured at the time of trial as DW 2. On behalf of the defendant No.1 local Tahsilder deposed as DW 1. One of the plaintiffs figured as PW 1 and to prove their possession they examined one Lakitullah who figured as PW 2.

9. The trial Court dismissed the suit on the finding "so in the absence of sufficient corroborative documentary evidence as regards the genuineness of the authentication and revalidation of the alleged power of attorney it cannot be held by any stretch of imagination that the alleged power of attorney is genuine. There is, so to say, no sufficient evidence on record in proof of the alleged contention that there was any valid or legal exchange of the 'A' schedule properties with that of the 'B' schedule properties by the respective owners thereof."

10. The trial Court has further observed that on the basis of the testimony of solitary witness PW 2, plaintiff's claim of possession of the properties in schedule 'A' "cannot be given any consideration in the absence of reliable and competent witnesses in this regard." It may be mentioned witness deposed on behalf of the defendant No.1 has stated that he has no personal knowledge as regard possession of the property in any respect. The trial Court on consideration of evidence of DW 2 has observed, "though it is found the deposition of this witness that his all other relations including his family members are inhabitants of India so it has now got to be ascertained whether DW 2 came over here at the instance of certain interested persons depose in this suit". It may be mentioned this witness came in the then East Pakistan in the month of February 1971 from Agartala in the State of Tripura, India upon obtaining a Pakistani passport. The trial Court has also observed "the plaintiffs have absolutely failed to sustain the alleged contention of making any exchange of the schedule properties with the owner of the 'A' schedule properties." The trial court lastly, observed "The plaintiffs thus have no locus standi in the suit." As against the judgment and decree of the court of first instance plaintiffs went on appeal. The appellate Court allowed the appeal and consequent thereupon reversing the judgment and decree of the court of first instance decreed the suit on the findings the defendant Nos. 6-12 did not place any material in support of their claim on the record nor any of them has deposed either in support of their claim or in denial or refusal of the claim and averments made by the plaintiffs in their pleading in support of the relief prayed for in the suit, that defendant No.5 who deposed as DW 2 came in the then Pakistan on February 25, 1971 upon obtaining a Pakistani passport and that after deposing in the suit upon taking back the passport he left the then Pakistan and that in his deposition he admitted that his sons and wife were staying in India and this aspect of the matter clearly shows that defendant Nos. 5-12 upon exchanging the properties had migrated to India and that after the exchange defendant Nos. 5-12 have no right, title and interest in the land described in schedule 'A', that there is no reliable material on record in support of the finding of the trial Court that irrevocable power of attorney in the form of deed of exchange, Exhibit 1 is forged and collusive, that on examination of the Exhibit I it is seen that the same was registered by the Munsif-cum-Magistrate of Udaypur in Tripura State, India on May 24, 1963 and that on scrutiny of the document there is nothing therein wherefrom the same ie Exhibit 1, can be said to be forged and collusive, that it cannot be said that the document Exhibit 1 is forged and fabricated as because the same was revalidated and re-stamped by the Office of the Deputy Commissioner, (Revenue) Comilla and that since respondent No. 11who contested the suit has not brought on record any material to show that at the relevant time Deputy Commissioner, Noakhali was authorised to revalidate and re-stamp exchange deed between the migrant from India and the migrant from the then East Pakistan and, as such, no exception can be taken as regard revalidation and re-stamping of Exhibit 1 from the office of Deputy Commissioner (Revenue) Comilla and that revalidation and re-stamping was made under the signature of Additional Deputy Commissioner, (Revenue) Comilla and that in the background of the said fact the contesting respondents (defendant Nos. 1 and 5) did not bring on record any material to show that the signature appearing in Exhibit 1 was not of the Additional Deputy Commissioner (Revenue) of the relevant time ie 6-12-1963, that as Exhibit 1 bears the signature of the Munsif-cum- Magistrate of Udaypur, Tripura State, India and the Additional Deputy Commissioner (Revenue), Comilla, as such, it cannot be said that Ex. 1 is forged and collusive. From the contesting defendants' side no evidence has been led in refusal of the evidence produced by the plaintiffs in support of their claim of being in possession of the land since August 1963 pursuant to the exchange that took place between the plaintiffs and the defendant Nos. 5-12. It has neither been claimed nor proved by the defendant No.1 that after declaring the properties in schedule 'A' as evacuee/enemy property the said authority took possession of the same and that itself managed or leased out the same or that is managing the same itself in any mode or manner. It is also not the case of the defendant Nos. 5-12 in their pleadings or before the court that plaintiffs entered into the land forcibly upon ousting them and that since claim of possession of the plaintiffs in the land in suit has not been disproved from the side of the defendants the irresistible conclusion is that they came into possession of the land in suit on the basis of Exhibit 1 ie irrevocable power of attorney, in the form of deed of exchange and that for the last 30 years they are in possession of the land on the basis of the Exhibit 1 and that on the basis of continuous possession for 30 years, plaintiffs have acquired interest in the land and, as such, entitled to the relief sought for.

11. Thereupon the contesting defendant No.5, the heirs of non-contesting defendants Nos. 7 and 8 (defendant-petitioner Nos. 1-5 in the leave petition) non-contesting defendants Nos. 9-12 as well as the non-contesting some other defendants (added defendants) who figured in the revisional application as petitioner Nos. 11-14 moved the High Court Division in revisional jurisdiction and obtained Rule. The High Court Division discharged the Rule on the finding, "The very fact that the defendant No.5 came in 1971 in the month of February with Pakistani passport shows that he was in India and he exchanged his property along with other brothers with those of the plaintiffs in India which have been fully described in schedule 'B' to the plaint...... It is also to be noted that although the other defendants filed written statement but except the defendant No.5 none deposed in support of their respective case. It is true that it is the plaintiffs who are to prove their case and they cannot succeed on the weakness of the defendant's case, but when the plaintiffs filed the registered power of attorney as the basis of their possession in the suit land and when the contesting defendant challenged the said power of attorney and the exchange in pursuant thereto he had some onus to prove assertions as to his case of living in Bangladesh and possession in the suit land which he has failed to prove. Similar is the case with the defendant No.1 namely, the Government......... ... the Government did not assert that they took possession of the suit property namely, the 'A' scheduled property, after its owners left this country and have been possessing the same through the lessees The trial Court, in fact, did not come to any finding to the factum of possession of the suit land by the plaintiffs which is very crucial in the facts and circumstances of the instant case and discarded the evidence of PW 2 on the ground that he was the solitary witness as to the possession of the suit land in support of the plaintiff's case of possession since 1963, completely overlooking the provision of section 134 of the Evidence Act and further fact that the plaintiff's possession was never denied by the contesting defendants herein as discussed hereinabove. In .the facts and circumstances of the case and the evidence on record, and that particularly the fact that the plaintiffs are in possession of the suit land since 1963 by virtue of the registered power of attorney, I am of the view that the plaintiffs have acquired a right to the 'A' scheduled property at least to protect their possession to maintain a suit within the meaning of section 42 of the Specific Relief Act and their suit is maintainable." The learned Judge on examining the Exhibit 1, irrevocable power of attorney placed before the Court by the learned Advocate for the plaintiffs opposite-party, has observed," from a mere look with a bare eye it appears that the same was registered in the Court of Munsif, Udaypur and was validated by the Deputy Commissioner, Comilla." The appellate Court also on consideration of evidence as well as on scrutiny of Exhibit 1 held the same as genuine.

12. The leave petition has been filed by the heirs of non-contesting defendant Nos. 7 and 8 (petitioner Nos. 1-5) the non-contesting defendant Nos. 10-12, non-contesting subsequent transferees (petitioner Nos. 10-12) and the contesting defendant No.5. The learned Counsel for the petitioners submits that Exhibit 1-irrevocable power of attorney in the form of deed of exchange-is a spurious document and that the said Exhibit 1 cannot be treated as a document of title creating interest in the immovable property and that this fact has not been noticed by the High Court Division as well as the appellate Court and thus has caused failure of justice, that the irrevocable power of attorney as was not endorsed by the then Pakistan High Commission of India and, as such, no credence as could be given to that both High Court Division and the Court of appeal below erred in treating power of attorney as the basis of right, that the High Court Division has affirmed the judgment of the Court of appeal below upon reversing the judgment and decree of the trial Court without considering the total materials on record and that the appellate Court arrived at the erroneous decision upon the wrong presumption on a false and forged power of attorney which is not a document of title and that fact of execution and due authentication and registration having not been duly established, that from the plaintiffs' side no material has been placed on record as to why the Exhibit 1 was revalidated and re-stamped in the Office of the Additional Deputy Commissioner (Revenue) Comilla while the property in schedule 'A' which plaintiffs claim to have got on the basis of their exchange of the property described in schedule 'B' in the Tripura State, India is undisputedly the properties situate in the District of Noakhali, that the High Court Division as well as the appellate Court wrongly shifted the onus upon the defendants relating to revalidation and re-stamping of the Exhibit 1 in Comilla, that High Court Division as well as appellate Court were in error in drawing up the presumption of genuineness, of Exhibit 1 on the finding that the plaintiffs are in possession of the land although plaintiffs in support of their claim of possession have examined solitary witness PW 2, that High Court Division as well as the court of appeal below were in error in holding that Exhibit 1 was authenticated by the Office of the Deputy Commissioner (Revenue), Comilla although there is no reference in Exhibit 1 of any case number in initiation where of the document was revalidated and re-stamped, that High Court Division as well as the court of appeal below were in serious error in holding that the plaintiffs are in possession of the 'A' scheduled land for long 30 years on the basis of Exhibit 1.

13. The plaintiff upon asserting their claim on the basis of Exhibit 1 irrevocable power of attorney in the form of deed of exchange, filed the suit seeking declaration against the notification issued on 31-7-1965 and published in the Gazette on 4 November, 1965 by the then Government of East Pakistan treating the property as evacuee/enemy property that the property described in schedule-A was not evacuee/enemy property and that the notification published in the Gazette on 4 November, 1965 declaring the property as evacuee/enemy property is illegal, without jurisdiction and not binding upon them.

14. Although 4 sets of defendants ie defendant Nos. 1, 5, 6 and 7-12, filed separate written statements but finally, the suit was contested by the defendant Nos. 1 (respondent No.5 herein) and 5 (herein petitioner No.6) and from the defendant No. 18 side local Tahsilder has deposed as DW 1 who in his deposition has frankly stated that he has no idea about the possession of the land of schedule 'A'. Defendant No.5 figured in the suit as DW 2 and he has not said anything denying plaintiff's claim of possession as deposed by PWs 1 and 2.

15. The plaintiffs are claiming the land on the basis of Exhibit 1 and that in support of their claim of possession plaintiff No.1 has deposed in the case as PW 1 and that have examined another witness ie PW 2 who has corroborated the PW 1 on the question of possession of the land in 'A' schedule by the plaintiffs.

<u>16. The contention of the defendant No.5 was that plaintiffs used to go from Noakhali to Tripura State and that used to work there as seasonal labour and as such the question of their having land as described in schedule 'B' in the Tripura State was a myth. This contention of the defendant No.5 has not been established by placing any material on record. The plaintiffs are claiming the land on the basis of Exhibit 1. Fact of plaintiffs being in possession of the land of schedule 'A' has not been specifically denied by the non-contesting defendant Nos. 6-12 in their pleadings. The lone contesting defendant No.5 also in specific term has not denied the possession of the plaintiffs either in his pleading or in his deposition. From the side of the contesting defendants there is no evidence in denial of the claim of possession of the land described in schedule 'A' to the plaint by the plaintiffs. The fact of possession of the plaintiffs in the 'A' schedule land has been found on the basis of the evidence on record by the High Court Division as well as the court of appeal below. The learned Counsel for the petitioners has not been able to point out any infirmity in the finding of the High Court Division as well as of the court of appeal below relating to the possession of the land described in 'A' scheduled by the plaintiffs. The learned Counsel for the petitioners could also not point out any misreading of the evidence relating to the finding as to possession of the 'A' schedule land by the plaintiffs arrived at by the High Court Division and the court of appeal below. It has been submitted by the learned Counsel for the petitioners that Exhibit 1 is a spurious document and that no ordinance should have been given to the same since the same was not endorsed by the then Pakistan High Commissioner in India and further, that Exhibit I was revalidated and re-stamped by the Office of the Additional Deputy Commissioner, (Revenue) Comilla although property described in 'A' Schedule to Exhibit 1 is of the District of Noakhali. A registered document carries presumption of correctness of the endorsement made therein and that one who disputes the said presumption is under the law required to dislodge the correctness of the endorsement in the registered document. Exhibit I has been registered by the Munsif-cum-Magistrate of Udaypur, Tripura State, India. Since defendant No. 5 was disputing the genuineness of the registered document Exhibit 1 it was his duty to establish that there was nothing like Munsif Magistrate, Official or Office in Udaypur in the Tripura State who was authorized to register irrevocable power of attorney. But the said defendant totally failed to bring on record any material wherefrom it can said Munsif Magistrate, Udaypur, Tripura State, India was not competent to register Exhibit 1. The fact is that Exhibit 1 was revalidated and re-stamped by the Office of the Additional Deputy Commissioner, (Revenue) Comilla. Official act has, the presumption of correctness and that one who challenges or disputes that presumption of correctness is required to establish that by legal evidence. From the defendants side nothing has been brought on record to show that Additional Deputy Commissioner, (Revenue), Comilla was not the authorised officer for revalidating and re-stamping the document like Exhibit 1 relating to the property of the Zone ie Comilla-Noakhali, obtained by a migrant from India to then East Pakistan. Defendant No.1, the Government of Bangladesh, contested the suit by filing written statement and examining DW 1. DW 1 has not said anything about the incompetency or impropriety of re-validation and re-stamping of Exhibit 1 by the Additional Deputy Commissioner, (Revenue) Comilla, nor the witness has stated that at the relevant time document like Exhibit 1 wherein property of Noakhali as is being claimed by the migrant from India upon exchanging their property with the migrant from the then East Pakistan to India, the Deputy Commissioner (Revenue), Noakhali was vested with the authority to revalidate and re-stamp document like Exhibit 1. So, the contention of the learned Counsel for the petitioners that revalidating and re-stamping of Exhibit 1 by the Additional Deputy Commissioner, (Revenue) Comilla without noting the case number on initiation which the said revalidation and re-stamping was made is an element of forgery and collusiveness of the document is of no substance. The High Court Division as well as the court of Appeal below on examination and scrutiny of Exhibit 1 have arrived at the finding that the same is genuine since it has been registered by the Munsif Magistrate, Udaypur, Tripura State,. India and that revalidated and re- stamped by the office of the Additional Deputy Commissioner, (Revenue) Comilla upon affixing official seal and signing the name of the officer who re-stamped and revalidated the Exhibit 1. In Exhibit. 1 there is clear description of the properties ie properties described in the 'B' schedule to the plaint, which the plaintiff gave to the defendants in exchange of the properties as described in the schedule 'A' to the plaint of which defendants were the owners. So, it was the duty of the defendants to establish either that the property as described in schedule 'B' to the plaint are fictitious property or that although plaintiffs are claiming the said properties but, in fact, they did not own the said properties or they had no right, title and interest in the property as described in schedule 'B' to the plaint. The contesting defendant No.5 has not taken any step to establish that the properties described in the schedule 'B' to the plaint were not of the plaintiffs while denying the plaintiffs' claim of exchanging 'B' schedule land with the 'A' schedule land. The High Court Division as well as appellate Court have concurrently held that the plaintiffs are in possession of the 'A' schedule land. The defendants miserably failed to establish that plaintiffs on the basis of Exhibit 1 are not in possession of the 'A' schedule land. The moot point for consideration is that had there been no exchange then how the plaintiffs went into possession of the land when there is no allegation from the side of the defendants that plaintiffs entered into possession of the land forcibly upon dispossessing the defendants. In our view, upon total consideration of the facts and circumstance of the case and that particularly the factum of possession of the land in suit ie 'A' schedule land, by the plaintiffs, the High Court Division as well as the court of appeal below were in no way in error in arriving at the finding that by Exhibit 1 there was exchange of the properties between the parties as described in Schedule 'A' and 'B' to the plaint and that on the basis of the exchange as evidenced by the Exhibit 1, the plaintiffs went into possession of the 'A' schedule land in August 1963 and they are in possession of the land and that have acquired interest in the land in suit, The defendants although contended that Exhibit 1 is a spurious document but in support thereof have not brought any material on record, rather the High Court Division and the appellate Court on examination and scrutiny of Exhibit 1 have held that the same is a genuine document and that there is no internal or external infirmity as regard the document for considering the same as not genuine.</u>

17. The High Court Division and the appellate Court noticed strange conduct of the defendant No, 5, herein petitioner No, 6, the lone contestant from amongst the defendant-exchangers, Although the properties in schedule 'A' to the plaint, which the plaintiffs got upon exchanging their properties described in schedule 'B' in Tripura State, India with the defendants No. 5-12, was declared evacuee property by notification dated 31-7-1965 which was published in the Gazette on November, 4, 1965 but none of the claimants ie defendants No, 5-12 had challenged the legality of the said notification and that accepting the said notification the defendant No, 5 had resisted the relief sought for by the plaintiffs in the suit It is pertinent to mention the trial Court although dismissed the suit of the plaintiffs but seriously doubted the bonafide of the contest put by the defendant No. 5 opposing the reliefs sought for in the suit by the plaintiffs upon noticing the fact that said defendant came to the then East Pakistan from Tripura state, India in the latter part of February, 1971 on a Pakistani passport and while deposing in court admitted plainly that at that time all the members of his family, that is, children and wife, as well as all the relatives were staying in Tripura State and other places of India and thereupon expressed view as to necessity of ascertaining the fact said defendant upon coming from Tripura State, India, was deposing at whose instance and for whose benefit. This conduct of the defendant No. 5 (DW 2) has quite legally been noticed by the trial Court that had the advantage of noticing his demeanour. The High Court Division and the appellate Court have quite legally taken into consideration the conduct of the defendant No.5 and the view expressed by the trial Court doubting bona fide of the said defendant putting opposition to the reliefs sought for in the suit by the plaintiffs.

<u>18. There is another important fact which was totally ignored by the trial Court while dismissing the suit, but noticed and considered by the High Court Division and the appellate Court in decreeing the suit. The same is factum of possession of the land in suit by the plaintiffs. The trial Court rejected the evidence led from the side of the plaintiffs on a queer and legally unsustainable ground and that was that PW 2 was the lone witness who deposed as regard the claim of possession of the plaintiffs in the land in suit being quite unmindful of the fact that the evidence of the PW 2, first was the corroborative evidence of PW 1 (one of the plaintiffs) who deposed about the fact of being in possession of the land in suit obtained on the basis of exchange in 1963 and without interruption possessing the land described in schedule 'A' to the plaint and second, if evidence of said witness is free from infirmity of any kind making not liable to be doubtful or, in other words, was of worth of taking into consideration for arriving at the decision as to matter of fact of possession then in law the evidence of said witness could have been basis for decision as regard the contention of the parties relating to possession of the land in suit. The reliability of the evidence of PW 2 has not been doubted by the trial Court. The position of law is that if a witness is otherwise found one of the kind-reliable or independent or non-partisan or disinterested, then the evidence of the said lone witness can be taken as foundation in making decision as regard an issue in the case. In the instant case trial Court has not found PW 2 as of not one of the kind or category mentioned herein before. The learned Counsel for the petitioner has not pointed out any infirmity in the evidence of PWs 1 and 2 making them unworthy of relying by the court for making decision as regard the issues involved in the suit.</u>

19. When the DW 1 (witness examined by the defendant No.1-Government of Bangladesh) has expressed his lack of knowledge about the possession of the land in suit or, in other words, has not denied the claim of plaintiffs possession in the land in suit and that DW 2 (defendant No. 5) has not specifically denied the claim of possession of the plaintiffs in the land in suit, nor was there any case from the side of the defendants in their pleadings as well as in the court that plaintiffs went into possession of the land in suit forcibly ousting the defendants from the properties described in schedule 'A' to the plaint and, as such, in that steel of the matter plaintiffs claim corning to possession of the land in suit in year 1963 on the basis of exchange being an admitted fact from the side of the defendants and that also fact of possession having been established by the plaintiffs by reliable and credible evidence and consequent thereupon having had acquired right and interest of unassailable character the High Court Division and the appellate Court were not in error of any kind in decreeing the suit. In the background of the materials on record the High Court Division has not committed any error in holding that there was exchange of the 'A' schedule properties with the 'B' schedule properties by the Exhibit 1 and on the basis of exchange between the plaintiffs and the defendants No. 5-12, the plaintiffs went into possession of the land 30 years back.

20. The plaintiffs went into possession of the plaint 'A' schedule land on the basis of Exhibit 1- irrevocable power of attorney in the form of deed of exchange and the said fact of obtaining of the possession of plaint 'A' schedule land on consideration of the legal evidence on record has been found genuine. The possession was obtained 39 years back from now and the plaintiffs are in uninterrupted possession of the land. Except contending by the defendant No.1 that recorded tenants left the then Pakistan for India and the land in plaint a schedule was declared evacuee property by notification of July 1965 and the said notification was published in the Gazette of November 4, 1965 no material worthy of consideration has been brought on record to establish the fact that property tall could be treated evacuee or enemy property because of the fact plaintiffs are being in possession of the land in plaint 'A' schedule on the basis of Exhibit 1 from August, 1963. The defendant No.1 has not taken any step to dislodge the legal presumption, because of the revalidation and re-stamping of the Irrevocable Power of Attorney in the form of deed of exchange by the Additional Deputy Commissioner (Revenue) Comilla upon affixing official seal and putting signature, of the Exhibit 1. By possessing the land in plaint 'A' schedule for 39 years past as of now upon obtaining the same on the basis of Exhibit 1, which has been found genuine by the High Court Division as well as by the appellate Court, the plaintiffs have acquired right and interest which cannot be said indefeasible or, in other words, right and interest as have accrued to the plaintiffs in the land described in plaint 'A' schedule is indefeasible and that for the protection thereof the suit as framed can very much be maintained.

The learned Counsel entering into caveat for the plaintiffs-respondent has made submissions supporting the judgment and order of the High Court Division. In the background of the discussion made hereinabove we find no substance in this petition. Accordingly, the petition is dismissed.

End.
